This scientific view, with its early dialectical insight, and these theoretical abstractions drawn from things that are always changing and transforming, brought Ibn Sīnā face to face with two major questions.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
First: where does the movement of change and transformation that runs throughout the world come from?
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Second: how does matter, in human knowledge, become separated from its direct sensory connections and turn into purely rational knowledge?
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The natural sciences of Ibn Sīnā’s time had not yet developed far enough to let him answer these two questions entirely from within his own scientific and practical method.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Even so, he was able to glimpse parts of the answer to the second question.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
And understanding the relation between movement and existence helps lay the foundation for understanding the relation between thought and reality, and ultimately for solving the problem of knowledge.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Ibn Sīnā inherited a vast philosophical tradition drawn from many different civilizations.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
At the center of that tradition stood one great problem above all others: the origin of the world as a whole.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
He came to see that the two questions that occupied him—the origin of movement in the world and the source of abstract concepts in knowledge—ultimately led back to this same larger problem.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
So he turned directly to it in trying to solve the two major questions that recur throughout much of his philosophical system.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The natural-philosophical part of his work became a theoretical and practical study of the phenomena of nature.

But he was not able to explain the deepest nature of those phenomena entirely from within nature itself, independently of the metaphysical ideas that still dominated the philosophical tradition of his time.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Even so, one feature of Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics is extremely important.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
He refuses to surrender to purely subjective speculation about the world “beyond nature” and then project that speculation back onto the external world.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
That had been the approach of Plato and of Neoplatonism in their philosophical systems.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
With Ibn Sīnā, we see something close to the reverse.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The external world forces itself into his metaphysical thinking.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
As we will see, the results of his study of natural phenomena, and the conclusions he drew from scientific experiment, leave a clear mark on his metaphysical ideas.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The first thing we notice when Ibn Sīnā discusses matter and form is that, on the metaphysical side, he places them within the framework of the Neoplatonic theory of emanation.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
This already makes his treatment methodologically different from Aristotle’s, and that difference in method will also produce important differences in content.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
But even the framework of emanation does not remain the same as it was in Plotinus or in later Neoplatonism.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Ibn Sīnā gives it a form of his own.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Within this new framework, elements from Plotinus, the Stoics, and Aristotle are brought together.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Among the Aristotelian elements, matter and form occupy a particularly important place.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
This combination gives Ibn Sīnā a view of the external world that differs radically from Neoplatonism and also, in part—but in an important way—from Aristotle.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Neoplatonism treats essence as an “idea” and the sensory world as a product of that idea.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
This is where its strict idealism appears most clearly.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Aristotle, by contrast, begins from the sensory world itself and recognizes its real, objective existence.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Ibn Sīnā goes further than Aristotle in the direction of philosophical materialism.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Within the process of emanation, he gives matter and form a more active and effective role in bringing about the existence of the material world.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
He comes close to recognizing self-movement within things themselves, and to seeing movement as one of the forms in which matter exists.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
This marks an extremely important step in the materialist direction of his philosophy.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
It is joined by another step in the same direction: his recognition of a dialectical relation between matter and form in a way that works against the dualism Aristotle had imposed on that relation.

We will see this position in its fuller form through Ibn Sīnā’s own texts.

We now want to return to a point made a little earlier: Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics reflects conclusions he reached through both theoretical and practical study of the natural world.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
It is easy to see clear reflections of the categories and laws of the material world in the structure of his metaphysical system.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
These were categories and laws that he had reached through both scientific experiment and logical reasoning.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
When we examine his theories about existence, we find that he builds them from these same categories and laws.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

It is true that Ibn Sīnā describes “divine science” as “the science that investigates absolute existence, its attributes and its principles,” and says that this science ultimately reaches the point from which all the other sciences begin, so that “the principles of the other particular sciences are explained within this science.”
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
But this does not contradict what we have said.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Here Ibn Sīnā is simply defining the relationship between philosophy and the particular sciences that study specific kinds of existing things, such as the natural sciences.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Philosophy, as a science, deals with the most general laws and principles.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
These are the principles through which the different laws discovered by the particular sciences can be understood in relation to one another.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
But this does not mean that the universal principles studied by philosophy exist separately from natural and social phenomena and their specific laws.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Nor does it mean that philosophy creates these principles somewhere outside the world of natural and social phenomena.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
In reality, philosophical principles—their content, origins, direction, and contradictions—are the highly developed and complex result of the positions philosophers take toward the external world.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
And above all, they reflect their position toward social reality.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
So when we say that Ibn Sīnā begins his philosophy of existence from the categories and laws of the material world, we are not claiming that he is unique in this respect.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
This is the objective starting point of every philosophy and every philosopher.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
What distinguishes Ibn Sīnā is that he does not hide this starting point, ignore it, or bury it under subjective speculation that tries to cut itself off from reality.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Instead, he remains closely tied to the roots from which his “divine science” draws the principles that later become general principles for the particular sciences.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Ibn Sīnā gives us evidence of this connection in two ways.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
First, in the way he handles the principles of “divine science” in general.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Second, in the way he treats the theory of matter and form in particular.

The first can be seen in the subjects discussed in the opening section of the metaphysics in both al-Shifāʾ and al-Najāt, and in the third section of al-Ishārāt, which deals with metaphysics.

These subjects include a number of principles that Ibn Sīnā calls the “principles of physics.”
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
And they really are questions that express categories and laws drawn from the observation of natural phenomena themselves.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
He discusses them in the sections of his works devoted to “divine science” and uses them as the foundation for his metaphysical theories.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

He studies substance and accident, the one and the many, cause and effect, the meaning of the universal, the eternal and the created, sensible qualities, potentiality and actuality, condensation and rarefaction, and the relation between matter and form.

He examines all of these through their existence in nature and then draws general conclusions from them.

Those conclusions become the theoretical basis for his discussions in “divine science.”

The questions of substance and accident; the division of existence into necessary, possible, and impossible; its further division into eternal and created; the distinction within created existence between what is essential and what is temporal; and the question of matter and form together with the theory of causes—all of these are basic pillars of Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics.

But he places these pillars within the world of metaphysics only after developing them from broader conclusions drawn from his study of nature.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The case of matter and form is even clearer.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
First, the theory is closely connected with every one of the questions we have just mentioned.

Second, it is almost the central nerve of Ibn Sīnā’s entire theory of the cosmos.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
It is not enough to say that his general conclusions about matter and form grew out of the study of natural bodies.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
We also need to add that the role they play in his metaphysics is an extension and continuation of the material role they play in the natural world.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
Through this continuity, they help Ibn Sīnā present the world as one connected whole rather than as two separate worlds, one spiritual and the other material.

The eternal material unity of the world, as it appears in this philosophical system, resolves the contradiction and removes the dualism contained in Aristotle’s idea of the “unmoved mover.”

That idea ends the chain of motion in the eternal stillness of the first mover. This is the contradiction.

It also separates the fixed and unmoving world of the “mover” from the changing and transforming world of what is moved. This is the dualism.

And through both, Aristotle’s idealism appears despite some of the materialist starting points in his philosophy.

The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
How does this unity of the world appear in Ibn Sīnā’s philosophical system?
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
To answer that question clearly, we need to separate three interlocking parts of the problem and look at each in turn.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

The problem of necessary existence: Ibn Sīnā develops this question in his own independent way. His theory begins by dividing existence, in principle, into three kinds: what must exist, what can exist, and what cannot exist. But when he turns to what actually exists, only the first two remain.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

“Every existing thing, considered in itself and without reference to anything else, must be one of two things. Either existence belongs to it necessarily in itself, or it does not. If existence belongs to it necessarily, then it is the truth in itself [God], whose existence is necessary through itself, the Self-Subsisting. If existence does not belong to it necessarily, we cannot call it impossible in itself once we have already assumed that it exists.”
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

We call something impossible only when we assume that its cause does not exist. If its cause does exist, then its existence becomes necessary. But if we consider the thing simply in itself, apart from any such condition, then it is only possible.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
“Considered in itself, then, it is something whose existence is neither necessary nor impossible. Every existing thing is therefore either necessary in itself or possible in itself.”
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

But even this division between necessary and possible existence becomes purely theoretical once Ibn Sīnā divides necessary existence itself into two kinds: what is necessary in itself, and what is necessary through something else. As long as a possible thing actually exists, it becomes necessary through something else.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

And when we learn, in addition, that what is necessary through another is “eternally and always existent,” just like what is necessary in itself, then calling it merely “possible” becomes little more than a distinction we make in thought. It serves only to distinguish it, considered in itself, from what is necessary through itself. In actual existence, both are equally necessary.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

“Every possible existent either has its existence through itself or through some cause. If it exists through itself, then its essence is necessary in existence, not possible in existence. If it exists through a cause, then either its existence becomes necessary when the cause exists, or it remains as it was before the cause existed. The latter is impossible. Its existence must therefore become necessary when its cause exists. Thus everything that is possible in itself is necessary in existence through another.”
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
So there is no existing thing whose existence is not necessary.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
The distinction between what is necessary in itself and what is necessary through another now becomes a distinction based simply on the fact that the first is regarded as the cause of the second.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
And with that, the problem moves to another link.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

The problem of cause and effect: here we can expect an important development in the logic of Ibn Sīnā’s theory. The relationship between the Necessary Existent as cause and the necessary existent as effect will show us where the logic of the entire system is heading.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy

The first thing we find is that, in actual existence, the relationship rests on a kind of balance between cause and effect, despite the conceptual distinction between what is necessary in itself and what is necessary through another.
The Problem of Existence and Essence in Ibn Sīnā’s Philosophy
“The principle of all things is an essence whose existence is necessary, and what proceeds from the Necessary Existent must necessarily exist.”
